claims.text: Inhibiting atomic mobility during reduction governs the formation of noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Restricted mobility causes HEA nanoparticle formation to proceed according to stochastic principles.
The stochastic process produces random, homogeneous mixing of five or more noble-metal elements into a single phase.
Sequential reduction would otherwise induce phase separation.
The starting material is a solid or minimally solvated mixture of noble-metal single-source precursors.
Each precursor contains at least five elements.
Low-temperature reduction combined with rapid immobilization limits atomic mobility.
Limited mobility of reduced metal atoms forces random incorporation rather than segregation.
Inhibiting precursor mobility reduces atomic rearrangement and suppresses thermodynamically driven segregation.
Increasing the number of distinct metal elements statistically promotes random alloying and stabilizes a single-phase high-entropy structure.
Higher-mobility baseline conditions lead to phase segregation and elemental clustering.
Mobility-inhibiting conditions will produce a more homogeneous, single-phase HEA nanoparticle structure than higher-mobility conditions.
A homogeneous single-phase HEA can form even when elemental reduction is not strictly simultaneous.
Higher atomic mobility causes phase separation, elemental segregation, and non-uniform morphology in bimetallic or multielement nanoparticle systems.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems containing five or more elements and reduced through a single-source precursor approach.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when cooperative reduction naturally synchronizes atomic incorporation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to binary alloys because different kinetic factors dominate them.
The quantitative mobility limit required for homogeneous mixing is unknown.
The required mobility limit may scale with element count or particle size.

contradictions.description: The central variable alternates between mobility of reduced metal atoms and mobility of precursors. These are distinct physical quantities, so the proposed intervention and cited mechanism are not consistently defined.
